summary: An excerpt from a novel (labeled 'Book 10 — part 56') in which two characters talk on a beach while surfers come in. They discuss the narrator's Orthodox parents, who are atheists yet follow Biblical Law as a practical guide to life, and the narrator explains Jewish mourning customs: burial within 24 hours, which keeps mourners too busy to fall apart, followed by a structured period of home mourning. The dialogue is playful and banter-driven.
one_line: A beach conversation in a novel about atheist-Orthodox parents, the value of ritual, and Jewish mourning customs.
key_facts: The narrator says his parents are Orthodox but do not believe in God; they value Biblical Law as a way of negotiating life.
The narrator compares his atheist-Orthodox parents to Mennonites, saying they find the old ways a useful set of rules for navigating the universe's curves.
The narrator says that the ritual is the important part, including thinking good thoughts and having right mind.
The narrator argues that if you follow the Law, you get to where you're going, in good time, with little pain, even without knowing why.
She compares following the Law to following the ants, which she says go where they go and it works.
The narrator says Jews are on the melodramatic end of the grieving scale, with weeping, hair-tearing and throwing themselves on coffins.
Rabbinical scholars over about 5,000 years developed a protocol so that mourners grieve enough to avoid guilt but not so much that they become a drag on the tribe.
Under the protocol, the dead are usually buried within 24 hours.
The day before burial is spent calling everyone, booking travel, ordering caterers, picking a box, fielding calls, getting the rabbi and booking the limo, leaving no time to fall to pieces.
After burial, a family volunteer goes to the mourner's house to take the cushions off one of the sofas, hang sheets over the mirrors, and set out food.
The surfers come in from the water, jiggling and rebooting their boards and staring at a radical cutback off the lip.
She smiles and the narrator uses a tone of voice that signals he is avoiding telling her how wrong she is.
